text: Seven riddles. Sixty seconds each.
Some are easy. Some are sneaky.
Keep score in your head, and tell me your score at the end. Let's go.
Riddle number one.
A bat and a ball cost one dollar and ten cents in total.
The bat costs one dollar more than the ball.
How much does the ball cost?
You have sixty seconds. Pause the video if you need more time. Go!
Time's up! Did you say ten cents? That's the answer most people give first.
But if the ball cost ten cents, the bat would cost one dollar and ten cents, and together they would cost one dollar and twenty cents.
The real answer is five cents.
Five cents for the ball, plus one dollar and five cents for the bat: exactly one dollar and ten cents.
Psychologists use this very question to test whether we stop and check our first instinct.
Riddle number two.
A patch of lily pads doubles in size every single day.
On day forty-eight, it covers the whole lake.
On which day did it cover half the lake?
You have sixty seconds. Pause the video if you need more time. Go!
Time's up! The answer is day forty-seven.
If the patch doubles every day, then one day before the lake is full, it was exactly half full.
Many people say day twenty-four, because our brains think in straight lines, not in doublings.
That's why anything that keeps doubling, from bacteria to savings, can surprise us at the very end.
Riddle number three is where it gets trickier.
You have two ropes and a lighter.
Each rope takes exactly one hour to burn from end to end, but they burn unevenly: half a rope doesn't always take half an hour.
How can you measure exactly forty-five minutes?
You have sixty seconds. Pause the video if you need more time. Go!
Time's up! Here's the trick.
Light the first rope at both ends, and the second rope at one end, at the same time.
Burning from both ends, the first rope is gone in exactly thirty minutes, no matter how unevenly it burns.
At that moment, light the other end of the second rope.
It had thirty minutes of burning left, and now it burns from both ends, so it takes fifteen minutes.
Thirty plus fifteen: forty-five minutes.
Riddle number four.
In one of our Shorts, we showed that a pair of pants has two holes.
So how many holes does a T-shirt have?
One: four. Two: three. Three: zero.
You have sixty seconds. Pause the video if you need more time. Go!
Time's up! The answer is three.
A T-shirt has four openings: the neck, the bottom, and two sleeves.
Mathematicians who study shapes count tunnels you can pass through, and for a single piece like this, holes equal openings minus one.
Four openings minus one: three holes. Stretch the T-shirt without tearing it, and it flattens into a shape with three holes.
Riddle number five.
Imagine a rope wrapped tightly around the Earth's equator, almost twenty-five thousand miles long.
Now you add just three feet of rope, and lift it evenly all the way around the planet.
How high above the ground does it float? One: the width of a hair. Two: about six inches. Three: about a mile.
You have sixty seconds. Pause the video if you need more time. Go!
Time's up! The answer is about six inches.
A circle's length is two times pi times its radius, so adding three feet to the length raises the rope by three feet divided by two pi.
That's about five point seven inches, all the way around the Earth.
A mouse could walk under it. And here's the strange part: you'd get exactly the same gap around a basketball.
Riddle number six.
How many people do you need in a room for a better than fifty-fifty chance that two of them share a birthday?
One: twenty-three. Two: one hundred eighty-three. Three: three hundred sixty-six.
You have sixty seconds. Pause the video if you need more time. Go!
Time's up! The answer is just twenty-three.
It sounds far too small, because we imagine someone sharing our own birthday.
But with twenty-three people, there are two hundred fifty-three different pairs, and every pair is a chance for a match.
Put together, the odds pass fifty percent at twenty-three people. With seventy people, they're over ninety-nine percent.
And riddle number seven, the famous one that fooled even mathematicians.
On a game show, there are three doors. Behind one is a car. Behind the other two, goats.
You pick door number one. The host, who knows where the car is, opens door number three: a goat.
Should you stay with door one, or switch to door two? One: stay. Two: switch. Three: it doesn't matter.
You have sixty seconds. Pause the video if you need more time. Go!
Time's up! You should switch. Switching wins two times out of three.
When you first picked, you had a one in three chance of being right, and a two in three chance that the car was behind one of the other doors.
The host always opens a door with a goat, so he doesn't change your first chance. He just shows you which other door to take.
Stay, and you win one time in three. Switch, and you win two times in three.
When this puzzle ran in a magazine column in nineteen ninety, thousands of readers, including some with PhDs, wrote in to say the answer was wrong. It wasn't.
So, how many did you get right?
